New American Thoracic Society asthma guideline (Nov 2026): for adults and teens, relievers that contain an inhaled steroid are preferred over a salbutamol-only blue inhaler. Please don't switch on your own. Ask your doctor to review your inhaler plan. https://t.co/l9DwPDGIvR

LINKED PAGE (https://www.pulmonologyadvisor.com/features/ics-asthma-relievers-ats-guidelines/):
New clinical practice guidelines from the American Thoracic Society (ATS) recommend inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)-containing reliever therapy for adolescents and adults with asthma across the asthma severity spectrum. The new guidance was published in the American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine and addresses treatment with short-acting β₂-agonists (SABAs), ICS-containing relievers, and maintenance-and-reliever therapy (MART).
The ATS task force, comprising 16 asthma clinicians and researchers, 5 methodologists, and a patient representative, developed the guidance by evaluating 6 clinical questions addressing ICS-containing reliever therapy across asthma severity levels. Systematic literature reviews were conducted to assess the available evidence, and recommendations were formulated using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework.
For patients aged 12 years and older at National Asthma Education and Prevention Program (NAEPP) treatment Steps 1 and 2, the panel strongly recommends as-needed ICS-SABA over SABA alone, based on moderate-certainty evidence.
The recommendation was informed by findings from the BEST (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT00382889 ) and BATURA (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05505734 ) randomized controlled trials, with data from a total of 2664 participants contributing to the guideline’s evidence analysis. Compared with SABA alone, ICS-SABA significantly lowered the risk of severe exacerbations (risk ratio [RR], 0.55; 95% CI, 0.41-0.74), exacerbation rates (rate ratio, 0.47; 95% CI, 0.34-0.64), and emergency department visits (rate ratio, 0.43; 95% CI, 0.28-0.65). Systemic corticosteroid exposure was also reduced, with comparable overall adverse event rates between groups.
The panel conditionally recommends as-needed ICS plus SABA, delivered through combination or separate inhalers, over scheduled ICS plus as-needed SABA, based on low-certainty evidence.
In 3 randomized trials involving 667 patients, severe exacerbation risk did not differ significantly between treatment approaches (RR, 0.62; 95% CI, 0.05-7.74). However, patients receiving as-needed ICS plus SABA had lower cumulative ICS exposure and fewer nonserious adverse events. Scheduled ICS was associated with modest advantages in selected symptom-control outcomes.
The panel strongly recommends as-needed ICS-formoterol instead of SABA alone, based on moderate-certainty evidence.
Across 3 randomized trials (N=3052), researchers found that ICS- formoterol significantly reduced severe exacerbation risk (RR, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.35-0.59) and severe exacerbation rates (rate ratio, 0.36; 95% CI, 0.27-0.49). Treatment was also associated with fewer urgent medical visits, reduced oral prednisone exposure, and improved asthma control. However, the average improvement in Asthma Control Questionnaire scores remained below the threshold considered clinically meaningful.
For patients otherwise receiving scheduled ICS plus as-needed SABA, the panel conditionally recommends as-needed ICS-formoterol, based on low-certainty evidence.
Findings from 6 randomized trials (N=8195) showed no statistically significant difference in severe exacerbation risk between regimens (RR, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.62-1.04). As-needed ICS-formoterol was associated with lower inhaled and oral corticosteroid exposure. Although scheduled ICS offered slightly better results for certain symptom-control measures, the differences generally did not reach established thresholds for clinical importance.
Overall, the evidence supports ICS-containing reliever therapy (combined with formoterol or SABA), with reduction in exacerbations, lower CS exposure and a reassuring safety profile.
For patients aged 12 years and older at NAEPP Steps 3 through 5, the panel strongly recommends scheduled and as-needed ICS-formoterol as MART over maintenance ICS-long-acting β₂-agonist (LABA) plus as-needed SABA, based on moderate-certainty evidence.
